source.title: On the Generalization Power of Overfitted Two-Layer Neural Tangent Kernel Models
source.authors: Pei-Zhong Ju; Xiao-Jun Lin; N. Shroff

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error while varying neuron count in an overfitted two-layer NTK model, using a theoretical analysis and simulations rather than reproducing the original studies' full double-descent sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper's own figures and theoretical results on the two-layer NTK model are included. The Fourier-feature curves in Figure 1 are included as reported simulation comparators. Claims attributed to cited studies, including the cited results of Arora et al., are not recorded as this study's results. The paper does not sweep training epochs or sample size near the interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The paper sweeps neuron/feature count p in its own simulations. It measures test MSE for a min-ℓ2 NTK model, a GD-trained two-layer ReLU network and Fourier-feature models, and gives a bound showing NTK error keeps falling as p grows past interpolation. This is a different method aimed at the second-descent part of the claim. Every sweep sits in the overparameterized regime: Assumption p ≥ n/d, and plots start at p=100 with n=50, d=2, so the threshold is p=25. No peak is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that for learnable target functions, test error of overfitted two-layer NTK models keeps descending as p grows past interpolation. It approaches a small limit that shrinks with n, unlike simple Fourier/Gaussian-feature models whose error returns to null risk. For targets outside the learnable class (e.g. odd-power components), error is bounded away from zero for any n and p. They also find that the noise effect does not decrease with p. The Gaussian-feature contrast comes from a cited formula, not their own simulation.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes min-ℓ2 overfitting solutions for a two-layer, bias-free ReLU NTK under uniform spherical inputs and initial weights, and supplements bounds with simulations. It does not reproduce the original studies' full model-size, epoch, and sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on whether the ground-truth function is in the paper's learnable class; the reported curves also vary with noise level and with neuron count or training sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: For n=50, gaps between test-MSE curves at noise σ²=0, 0.04 and 0.16 do not shrink as p grows. At p=20000, the noisy-minus-noiseless difference is insensitive to n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In overfitted NTK models the noise contribution to test error does not vanish as width grows, unlike simple-feature linear models.

record.problems: The numerical results are presented in plots without tabulated values or reported uncertainty estimates. The model-size evidence is limited to a two-layer, bias-free ReLU NTK and particular target functions; the full fall-rise-fall shape is not measured.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results were left out. Theorem 1 and Proposition 2 provide bounds rather than separately measured model-by-condition outcomes; their conclusions are summarized in authors_conclusion and the labels.

untested.parts: The test-error peak near the interpolation threshold and the initial fall. Only p ≥ 100 > n/d = 25 is swept. Networks deeper than two layers.
Entire version; no test error over epochs.
Entire version; the sample sweep is far from the interpolation threshold.
The classical U-shaped region and the peak at interpolation; model classes beyond NTK, a two-layer net and Fourier features.
Entire version. Noise is varied only in the overparameterized region, and there is no regularization sweep or check for peak splitting.

record.verdict_notes: R1 is moved from V1 to V4 because the NTK model is linear. The Fourier rows are recast from reversed to partial because they descend before rising. No study result covers the interpolation peak, since all sweeps start well above p=n/d. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The full fall-rise-fall curve and the location of its peak near the training-set interpolation threshold are not established; the reported descent concerns the overparameterized region.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
The sample-size sweep uses p = 20000 and n from 20 to 100, not a setting near the interpolation threshold.
The comparisons cover the reported two-layer NTK and Fourier-feature simulations, not model classes generally.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
Noise levels are varied, but the study does not test whether noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: min-ℓ2 overfitting solution for the two-layer NTK model
rows.operation_detail: Varied neuron count p and measured test MSE.

conditions.value: learnable: f(θ) = sum over k ∈ {0,1,2,4} of (sin(kθ) + cos(kθ))

rows.baseline: null risk (error of the model that predicts zero)
rows.locator: Figure 1(a); Section 3, Descent in the overparameterized region
rows.note: The text says the test MSE confirms descent in the overparameterized region; the curve averages 9 simulation runs. The paper also notes oscillation at small p.
rows.check: The min-ℓ2 NTK solution is a linear model, not a deep network, so it bears on V4 rather than V1. Its descent is past interpolation only; the plotted range never reaches the threshold. The authors note oscillation at small p.

rows.baseline: null risk (error of the model that predicts zero)
rows.note: The text says the test error stays above null risk and looks different from the learnable-target case, but does not specify its trend with p. The curve averages 9 simulation runs.
rows.check: The p-trend is not described. The text says only that the curve stays above null risk and that Proposition 2 bounds the error away from zero. It belongs to V4, not V1, since the subject is the linear NTK model.
